1.station: The descent does not start where the route tops out. The rappel line begins roughly 30 m down and skier's right of the top-out, reached by walking and downclimbing from the summit exit, so hunt for it rather than rigging off the first thing at the finish.
1.pull: 60 m is the stated minimum rope for this line; a 70 m makes every station comfortable.

2.station: Top of the bolted line down the right side of the West Face. The first rappel drops straight down the face to a station described as a hanging belay with no ledge to stand on.
hazards: hanging station - get tethered in before unweighting the rope

3.station: Next bolted station down the face; from here the line is described as trending climber's left rather than falling straight down.
hazards: the line steps sideways here, so the next anchor is not directly below the rope

4.station: Commonly reported as the third rappel of the bolted sequence, and the tight one: on a 60 m rope parties describe reaching down to clip a tether to the anchor and then feeding rope through the device to close the last bit. One station on this line is described as a piton backed by a bolt rather than two bolts.
hazards: rope ends land in the working zone on a 60 m - knot both ends
mixed piton-and-bolt anchor at one station on this line; inspect before loading
4.pull: A 70 m rope removes the squeeze entirely.

5.station: Lowest station; the line puts you back essentially where packs are left at the base. Accounts differ on the bottom of the sequence - some describe the last one or two rappels off tree slings above and below the chimney rather than off bolts.
5.pull: Pulls on this line are reported clean and direct, but at least one rappel clears a roof, so expect the ends to hang free of the wall.

1.station: This is the classic line, not the bolted West Face one, and the two leave the summit from different places. Scramble down south and west of the summit, then down and skier's left toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire; the first fixed station is on that side.
hazards: committing to the wrong descent is the easy mistake here - the bolted West Face rappels start well away from this line

3.station: This rappel lands in the notch and Southwest Couloir between North and South Early Winters Spire.
hazards: the notch is often still snow-covered in summer - expect a wet or snowy stance and possibly a footwear change at the anchor

4.station: Fixed slings on the large chockstone blocking the couloir. The rappel goes off and past the chockstone and is largely free-hanging, about 50 ft of air.
hazards: free-hanging and spinning below the chockstone
the anchor is webbing around a natural feature rather than hardware - inspect it and replace or back it up
4.pull: Described as a double-rope rappel; check the pull before the second climber commits, since there is no way back up to the anchor once you are hanging free.

5.station: Short rappel of about 30 ft off a tree at the bottom of the couloir; scrambling and downclimbing is the accepted alternative if the tree or its slings look poor.

1.station: Reverse the ridge on easy downclimbing with short rappels through the steeper steps; this longer one drops back into the North Ridge Notch, the same notch gained on the approach.
hazards: cutting straight onto the West Ridge from higher up instead of dropping to the notch first is reported as looser with more rockfall potential

2.station: The West Ridge rappel sequence starts at an obvious two-bolt chain station just west of the summit; every station on this line is now bolted.
2.pull: A single 60 m rope covers each rappel of this sequence.

3.station: This is the station parties report losing. It sits off the crest rather than straight below - accounts place it variously on the north side of the ridge and out skier's left - and there is scattered old tat in the gully that is not the anchor. Look for bolts, not the first sling you see.
hazards: station easy to rappel straight past
old tat in the gully that reads as an anchor and is not the bolted line

4.station: This rappel ends on a flat part of the ridge crest.

5.station: Last station of the sequence; below it the ground turns to compact choss, kitty litter and a large scree bowl.
hazards: loose scree over slabs immediately below the last rappel
two southwest-facing gullies below the rappels pull parties in and cliff them out - stay out of them and look for the cairn marking the correct line
5.pull: Some parties add a short rappel off a tree just below the base of the ridge rather than downclimbing the scree.

1.station: There is no East Ridge descent. The rappels start from stations on the skier's-left / west side of the summit and follow the West Ridge crest down toward the base of the headwall; fixed anchor material on this line was reported replaced in mid-2024.
hazards: serious rockfall potential through the West Ridge section - keep the party off the fall line while ropes are being pulled
1.pull: Carry spare cord. The stations here are pins, nuts and slings maintained by whoever passes, and a party that arrives with nothing to leave gets stuck.

2.station: A large horn anchor, reached by scrambling down the ridge crest between rappels.

3.station: A three-pin anchor at the start of the ridge proper; the rappel from it goes down and climber's right off a large overhang.
hazards: free-hanging off the overhang, and the next station is offset to the side rather than straight below

5.station: Last of the West Ridge rappels. From its base the rope goes away briefly for a scramble down to a notch, and the South Face rappels begin from there.

6.station: First of the South Face rappels, starting at that notch.
hazards: several stations down this face are reached by traversing sideways - it cuts the rockfall exposure but makes it easy to swing past an anchor without seeing it, so look around before committing to the rope ends

14.station: The last rappel lands on a flat spot on the Terror Glacier.
hazards: you arrive on a glacier - rope up for crevasses before walking away from the anchor
14.pull: One account used every bit of a 70 m rope on this final rappel; a shorter rope means an extra station.

1.station: The descent is the West Ridge, not the South Face. The stations are on the skier's-left / west side of the summit; descend the ridge crest from there toward the base of the headwall.
hazards: accounts differ on how much fixed material is in place - some describe stations roughly a rope length apart on fixed pins, nuts and cord, reported replaced in mid-2024, while others describe building every anchor from gear. Carry cord and a rack for anchors either way.
1.pull: Loose blocks sit on this line; clear what you safely can rather than pulling ropes down onto it.

2.station: A large horn anchor, reached by scrambling down the ridge crest.

3.station: A three-pin anchor at the start of the ridge; the rappel from it goes down and climber's right off a large overhang.
hazards: free-hanging off the overhang, with the next station offset rather than straight below

4.station: Around here the line reaches the notch of the West Ridge gully and switches onto the South Face - one account counts about three and a half double-rope rappels down the ridge to just above that notch, then four more down the face.

7.station: The final rappel is short - about 100 ft in one account - off a slab anchor of two pins and a nut, landing back on the Terror Glacier above the bergschrund. On the South Face variant it returns you to the base of the route itself, so gear can be left there.
hazards: bergschrund immediately below the landing
rockfall onto the base of the route, which is where stashed packs sit
the wall overhangs enough on many pitches that the next station is not below you - plan on swinging in or leaving directional gear on nearly every rappel, and expect a free hang if you miss

7.station: This is the pitch that overhangs 40-plus feet. Without a line fixed on the way up you have to down-aid a long way to stay on the wall and reach the next station; sources note a 40 m line is long enough to fix here.
hazards: the biggest overhang on the route - rappelling it clean without a fixed line strands you off the wall

15.station: Pitch 15 is the one pitch without a bolted belay - the belay is gear, on a large ledge. The bolted rappel anchor is set far to the right along that ledge as you face the wall, not at the belay, so walk the ledge to find it.
hazards: arriving at the gear belay and looking for bolts that are not there is the trap on this station

16.pull: Strip any lines fixed during the ascent on the way down; leaving them is discouraged here and the buttress already carries old rope from previous attempts that should not be trusted.

1.station: The rappels do not reverse the route - they go over the top of the spire and drop into the descent gully on the far side, and only a few of them are needed before the gully becomes downclimbing.
hazards: the gully is steep and extremely loose, with rock coming down through it constantly - keep the party out of the fall line and clear of the ropes
1.pull: Published accounts give no per-station detail below this point. Budget 2.5-3 hours for the gully; parties benighted here describe about three hours of complex route-finding in the dark and advise against attempting it after dark.

wa_the_devils_club.skip_reason: Only one descent of this face has ever been documented, and everything that account records about it - the doubled/joined ropes, the first rappel hanging up and forcing a return to the top, the line angled toward the northeast ridge on the lower half, the rotten rock and the 3:30 a.m. finish - is already in the stored rappel data. No source locates any individual station, and the rappel line is built on the spot from natural anchors, so a per-station description would be invented rather than reported.
